Abstract.

We introduce Latin Eulerian numbers ⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle, a multivariate refinement of classical Eulerian numbers counting order-nn Latin squares by column ascents. We establish their fundamental symmetries, univariate marginals, and an exact multiplicity divisibility property. For the total ascent statistic Σ⁡(L)=∑iki​(L)\Sigma(L)=\sum_{i}k_{i}(L), we prove the sharp, isolated bounds n−1≤Σ⁡(L)≤(n−1)2n-1\leq\Sigma(L)\leq(n-1)^{2}, demonstrating that the adjacent values nn and (n−1)2−1(n-1)^{2}-1 are strictly unattainable. To analyze intermediate values, we show that symbol permutations typically ignored in classical enumeration directly govern Σ\Sigma via an exact formula. This insight yields explicit constructions for the interior range, motivates a unimodality conjecture for the total ascent distribution.

Key words and phrases: 
Eulerian numbers, Latin squares, permutation statistics, ascents, descents
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05A05, 05A15, 05B15

1. Introduction

The Eulerian numbers ⟨nk⟩\left\langle n\atop k\right\rangle, which count permutations π\pi of [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\} with exactly kk ascents (positions ii with π⁡(i)<π⁡(i+1)\pi(i)<\pi(i+1)), are among the most studied objects in enumerative combinatorics (see [1, 10, 11, 9]). Over the years, numerous refinements and generalizations of ⟨nk⟩\left\langle n\atop k\right\rangle have been introduced, including the qq-Eulerian numbers of Carlitz, the Eulerian numbers of type BB, and second-order Eulerian numbers on multiset permutations.

Another classical and richly developed domain in combinatorics is the theory of Latin squares. An order-nn Latin square is an n×nn\times n array with entries in [n][n] such that every row and every column contains each symbol exactly once. Euler himself initiated the systematic study of orthogonal Latin squares through his 3636 officers problem [4]; the resulting theory of orthogonal Latin squares, transversal designs, and quasigroups is surveyed in the standard reference of Dénes and Keedwell [2]. The number LnL_{n} of Latin squares of order nn is known exactly only for n≤11n\leq 11 [8], and no closed formula is known; the best asymptotic estimates come from the permanent-based approach following van der Waerden’s conjecture (proved by Egorychev [3] and Falikman [5]) and, more recently, from entropy methods of Linial and Luria [7].

It is natural to ask whether the two theories can be fruitfully combined. Because every column of a Latin square forms a permutation of [n][n], one may refine the enumeration of Latin squares by recording the number of ascents in each column simultaneously. This produces an nn-tuple of Eulerian-type statistics attached to every Latin square, and hence a genuinely multivariate array generalizing ⟨nk⟩\left\langle n\atop k\right\rangle. We call the resulting numbers Latin Eulerian numbers. Besides Euler’s own connection to both source concepts, the name is intended to signal that this array specializes, in a suitable sense, to nn independent copies of the classical Eulerian statistic, subject to the rigid combinatorial constraint of Latin-ness.

The purpose of this note is fourfold: (i) to define Latin Eulerian numbers and record their basic symmetries; (ii) to compute the array explicitly for n≤5n\leq 5; (iii) to establish sharp, isolated bounds for the total ascent statistic Σ=∑iki\Sigma=\sum_{i}k_{i} (Theorems 4.2 and 4.4) via a row-pair comparison argument; and (iv) to analyze how classical isotopy symmetries (row, column, and symbol permutations) control intermediate values of Σ\Sigma. Specifically, column permutations leave Σ\Sigma invariant (Proposition 2.5), restricted row permutations yield an explicit number-theoretic construction (§), and symbol permutations supply the decisive mechanism to bridge the remaining gap (Theorem 4.9). Finally, we present constructive evidence for a conjecture on interior coverage and unimodality (Conjecture 4.15).

2. Definitions and basic properties

Throughout, n≥2n\geq 2 is an integer and [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\}.

Definition 2.1.

For a permutation π\pi of [n][n], an ascent of π\pi is an index i∈{1,…,n−1}i\in\{1,\dots,n-1\} with π⁡(i)<π⁡(i+1)\pi(i)<\pi(i+1). We write asc⁡(π)\mathrm{asc}(\pi) for the number of ascents of π\pi, so 0≤asc⁡(π)≤n−10\leq\mathrm{asc}(\pi)\leq n-1 and ⟨nk⟩=#⁡{π∈Sn:asc⁡(π)=k}\left\langle n\atop k\right\rangle=\#\{\pi\in S_{n}:\mathrm{asc}(\pi)=k\}.

Definition 2.2.

An (order-nn) Latin square is a matrix L=(L⁡(i,j))1≤i,j≤nL=(L(i,j))_{1\leq i,j\leq n} with entries in [n][n] such that each row and each column of LL is a permutation of [n][n]. Let ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n} denote the set of order-nn Latin squares, and Ln=|ℒn|L_{n}=|\mathcal{L}_{n}|.

Definition 2.3.

For L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n} and 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, let ci​(L)=(L⁡(1,i),L⁡(2,i),…,L⁡(n,i))c_{i}(L)=(L(1,i),L(2,i),\dots,L(n,i)) be the ii-th column of LL, viewed as a permutation of [n][n], and set ki​(L)=asc⁡(ci​(L))∈{0,…,n−1}k_{i}(L)=\mathrm{asc}(c_{i}(L))\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}. For a composition 𝐤=(k1,…,kn)∈{0,…,n−1}n\mathbf{k}=(k_{1},\dots,k_{n})\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}^{n}, the Latin Eulerian number ⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle is

⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩=#{L∈ℒn:ki(L)=ki for all i=1,…,n}.\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle\;=\;\#\bigl\{\,L\in\mathcal{L}_{n}\;:\;k_{i}(L)=k_{i}\text{ for all }i=1,\dots,n\,\bigr\}.
Example 2.4.

For n=3n=3 the Latin square L=(123312231)L=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\ 3&1&2\\ 2&3&1\end{pmatrix} has columns (1,3,2)(1,3,2), (2,1,3)(2,1,3), (3,2,1)(3,2,1), with respectively 11, 11, 00 ascents. Hence LL is one of the squares counted by ⟨⟨31,1,0⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle 3\atop 1,1,0\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle.

Now, we record three elementary but structurally important properties column-permutation symmetry (Proposition 2.5), row-reversal symmetry (Proposition 2.6), and total mass (Proposition 2.7) of Latin Eulerian numbers.

Proposition 2.5.

For every permutation τ\tau of [n][n] and every composition 𝐤\mathbf{k},

⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩=⟨⟨nkτ⁡(1),…,kτ⁡(n)⟩⟩.\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle\;=\;\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop k_{\tau(1)},\dots,k_{\tau(n)}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle.

In particular, ⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle depends only on the multiset {k1,…,kn}\{k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\}.

Proof.

Permuting the columns of LL according to τ\tau (i.e. replacing LL by L′L^{\prime} with L′​(⋅,τ⁡(i))=L⁡(⋅,i)L^{\prime}(\cdot,\tau(i))=L(\cdot,i)) is a bijection ℒn→ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n}\to\mathcal{L}_{n}, and it carries a square with column-ascent vector (k1,…,kn)(k_{1},\dots,k_{n}) to one with column-ascent vector (kτ−1​(1),…,kτ−1​(n))(k_{\tau^{-1}(1)},\dots,k_{\tau^{-1}(n)}); since τ\tau ranges over all of SnS_{n} so does τ−1\tau^{-1}. ∎

Proposition 2.6.

The Latin Eulerian numbers satisfy the identity

⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩=⟨⟨nn−1−k1,…,n−1−kn⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop n-1-k_{1},\dots,n-1-k_{n}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle

for all 0≤k1,…,kn≤n−10\leq k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\leq n-1.

Proof.

Reversing the order of the rows of LL (row i↦i\mapsto row n+1−in+1-i) is a bijection ℒn→ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n}\to\mathcal{L}_{n} which turns every ascent of every column into a descent and vice versa, replacing kik_{i} by (n−1)−ki(n-1)-k_{i}. ∎

Proposition 2.7.

The sum of the Latin Eulerian numbers over all possible ascent tuples equals the total number LnL_{n} of Latin squares of order nn, means

∑𝐤∈{0,…,n−1}n⟨⟨nk1,…,kn⟩⟩=Ln.\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}^{n}}\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop k_{1},\dots,k_{n}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=L_{n}.
Proof.

This follows immediately, as every Latin square of order nn uniquely determines its ascent tuple 𝐤∈{0,…,n−1}n\mathbf{k}\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}^{n}. ∎

Proposition 2.7 is the sense in which Latin Eulerian numbers refine LnL_{n}, exactly as ⟨nk⟩\left\langle n\atop k\right\rangle refines n!=∑k⟨nk⟩n!=\sum_{k}\left\langle n\atop k\right\rangle; since no closed form for LnL_{n} is known, none should be expected in general for ⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle either, and we do not attempt one. We instead study the array computationally for small nn and analytically through the derived statistic Σ⁡(L)=∑iki​(L)\Sigma(L)=\sum_{i}k_{i}(L).

Our final basic property establishes that the univariate marginals of the Latin Eulerian array coincide with the classical Eulerian numbers, scaled by the factor Ln/n!L_{n}/n!.

Theorem 2.8.

Fix a column index i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\} and k∈{0,…,n−1}k\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}. Then

∑𝐤′:ki′=k⟨⟨n𝐤′⟩⟩=Lnn!⟨nk⟩.\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\,:\,k^{\prime}_{i}=k\end{subarray}}\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}^{\prime}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle\;=\;\frac{L_{n}}{n!}\,\left\langle n\atop k\right\rangle.
Proof.

It suffices to show that, among the LnL_{n} Latin squares of order nn, each of the n!n! permutations of [n][n] occurs as column ii equally often, namely Ln/n!L_{n}/n! times; summing this over the ⟨nk⟩\left\langle n\atop k\right\rangle permutations with exactly kk ascents gives the stated formula.

Fix two permutations σ,σ′∈Sn\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}\in S_{n} and let ρ=σ−1​σ′\rho=\sigma^{-1}\sigma^{\prime}. Given a Latin square LL with column ii equal to σ\sigma, define L′L^{\prime} by L′​(j,c)=L⁡(ρ⁡(j),c)L^{\prime}(j,c)=L(\rho(j),c) for all rows jj and columns cc; this is again a Latin square, since reordering the rows of a Latin square (here, by the permutation ρ\rho of row indices) preserves the Latin property. Its ii-th column satisfies L′​(j,i)=L⁡(ρ⁡(j),i)=σ⁡(ρ⁡(j))=σ⁡(σ−1​σ′​(j))=σ′​(j)L^{\prime}(j,i)=L(\rho(j),i)=\sigma(\rho(j))=\sigma(\sigma^{-1}\sigma^{\prime}(j))=\sigma^{\prime}(j), so column ii of L′L^{\prime} is exactly σ′\sigma^{\prime}. The map L↦L′L\mapsto L^{\prime} is invertible (apply the same construction with ρ−1=σ′−1​σ\rho^{-1}=\sigma^{\prime-1}\sigma), so it is a bijection between {L∈ℒn:column ​i​ of ​L=σ}\{L\in\mathcal{L}_{n}:\text{column }i\text{ of }L=\sigma\} and {L∈ℒn:column ​i​ of ​L=σ′}\{L\in\mathcal{L}_{n}:\text{column }i\text{ of }L=\sigma^{\prime}\}. As σ,σ′\sigma,\sigma^{\prime} were arbitrary, all n!n! classes have equal size, and since they partition ℒn\mathcal{L}_{n}, each has size Ln/n!L_{n}/n!. ∎

3. The array for n≤5n\leq 5

Using an exhaustive backtracking search over Latin squares (equivalently, over sequences of rows extending a partial Latin rectangle), we computed ⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle completely for n=3,4,5n=3,4,5. By Proposition 2.5 it suffices to tabulate one representative composition per multiset.

For n=3n=3 (L3=12L_{3}=12) there are exactly two nonzero multisets, related by Proposition 2.6:

⟨⟨32,1,1⟩⟩=⟨⟨31,2,1⟩⟩=⟨⟨31,1,2⟩⟩=2,⟨⟨30,1,1⟩⟩=⟨⟨31,0,1⟩⟩=⟨⟨31,1,0⟩⟩=2.\left\langle\!\!\left\langle 3\atop 2,1,1\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=\left\langle\!\!\left\langle 3\atop 1,2,1\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=\left\langle\!\!\left\langle 3\atop 1,1,2\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=2,\qquad\left\langle\!\!\left\langle 3\atop 0,1,1\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=\left\langle\!\!\left\langle 3\atop 1,0,1\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=\left\langle\!\!\left\langle 3\atop 1,1,0\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=2.

Notably, the “balanced” composition (1,1,1)(1,1,1) does not occur among order-33 Latin squares.

For n=4n=4 (L4=576L_{4}=576), the nonzero multisets and their common value (constant on each multiset, by Proposition 2.5) are shown in Table 1.

For n=5n=5 (L5=161280L_{5}=161280) there are 3939 nonzero multisets; the data are consistent with Propositions 2.5 and 2.7, in every case (each multiset gives a constant value on all of its arrangements, reversal-paired multisets share the same value, and all subtotals sum to 161280161280). The most balanced composition, (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2), is the unique maximiser among individual compositions, with value 64806480.

The values in Table 1 are conspicuously divisible by small numbers (66 appears six times, 64=2664=2^{6}, and so on); we now show this is not a coincidence but an exact structural fact, valid for every nn and every composition.

For a composition κ=(k1,…,kn)\kappa=(k_{1},\dots,k_{n}), let m1,…,mrm_{1},\dots,m_{r} denote the multiplicities of its rr distinct entries, so that m1+⋯+mr=nm_{1}+\cdots+m_{r}=n.

Theorem 3.1.

For every composition κ=(k1,…,kn)\kappa=(k_{1},\dots,k_{n}) with multiplicities m1,…,mrm_{1},\dots,m_{r},

∏i=1rmi!|⟨⟨nκ⟩⟩.\prod_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}!\;\Big|\;\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\kappa\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle.
Proof.

If ⟨⟨nκ⟩⟩=0\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\kappa\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=0 there is nothing to prove, so suppose LL is a Latin square with column-ascent vector κ\kappa. For τ∈Sn\tau\in S_{n} let τ⋅L\tau\cdot L be the Latin square with (τ⋅L)​(i,j)=L⁡(i,τ−1​(j))(\tau\cdot L)(i,j)=L(i,\tau^{-1}(j)), i.e. column jj of τ⋅L\tau\cdot L is column τ−1​(j)\tau^{-1}(j) of LL; this is a group action of SnS_{n} on the set of order-nn Latin squares by column permutation. The action is free: if τ⋅L=σ⋅L\tau\cdot L=\sigma\cdot L then column τ−1​(j)\tau^{-1}(j) of LL equals column σ−1​(j)\sigma^{-1}(j) of LL for every jj, and since the nn columns of a Latin square are pairwise distinct (two equal columns would force a repeated entry in some row), this forces τ−1=σ−1\tau^{-1}=\sigma^{-1}, i.e. τ=σ\tau=\sigma.

The column-ascent vector of τ⋅L\tau\cdot L is (kτ−1​(1),…,kτ−1​(n))(k_{\tau^{-1}(1)},\dots,k_{\tau^{-1}(n)}). Let H≤SnH\leq S_{n} be the subgroup of permutations that fix the tuple κ\kappa under this action, i.e. that permute only among positions sharing a common value; HH is the Young subgroup Sm1×⋯×SmrS_{m_{1}}\times\cdots\times S_{m_{r}}, of order ∏imi!\prod_{i}m_{i}!. By freeness, the orbit H⋅LH\cdot L consists of exactly |H|=∏imi!|H|=\prod_{i}m_{i}! distinct Latin squares, all with column-ascent vector κ\kappa.

The same argument applies to any Latin square L′L^{\prime} with column-ascent vector κ\kappa: its HH-orbit again has size exactly ∏imi!\prod_{i}m_{i}! and lies entirely within the fibre {L′:column-ascent vector of ​L′​ is ​κ}\{L^{\prime}:\text{column-ascent vector of }L^{\prime}\text{ is }\kappa\}. Two such HH-orbits are either equal or disjoint, so this fibre of size ⟨⟨nκ⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\kappa\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle is partitioned into blocks of size ∏imi!\prod_{i}m_{i}!, proving the divisibility. ∎

Definition 3.2.

For an achievable composition κ=(k1,…,kn)\kappa=(k_{1},\dots,k_{n}) with entry multiplicities m1,…,mrm_{1},\dots,m_{r}, the normalized Latin Eulerian number O⁡(n,κ)O(n;\kappa) is defined by

O⁡(n,κ)=⟨⟨nκ⟩⟩∏i=1rmi!.O(n;\kappa)=\frac{\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\kappa\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle}{\prod_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}!}.

Unwinding the proof of Theorem 3.1, O⁡(n,κ)O(n;\kappa) has a direct meaning: it is the number of orbits of the full column-permutation action of SnS_{n} on the set of Latin squares whose column-ascent multiset equals that of κ\kappa-equivalently, the number of Latin squares with that ascent-partition, counted up to reordering of columns. This separates ⟨⟨nκ⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\kappa\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle into an elementary, fully understood factor ∏imi!\prod_{i}m_{i}! and a residual quantity O⁡(n,κ)O(n;\kappa) which captures whatever is genuinely difficult about the count.

Table 2 confirms Theorem 3.1 without exception, and shows that O⁡(n,κ)O(n;\kappa) varies over a wide range even at n=5n=5: it equals 11 for six compositions (meaning every Latin square with that ascent-partition is a column permutation of a single example), while the most balanced partition {2,2,2,2,2}\{2,2,2,2,2\} has 5454 orbits and the largest value, {1,2,2,2,3}\{1,2,2,2,3\}, has 292292. Reversal-paired partitions (Proposition 2.6) always share the same value of OO, as the table shows (e.g. {0,1,1,1,1}\{0,1,1,1,1\} and {2,3,3,3,3}\{2,3,3,3,3\} both give O=1O=1). We regard O⁡(n,κ)O(n;\kappa), rather than ⟨⟨nκ⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\kappa\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle itself, as the natural object for further study: it isolates exactly the part of the enumeration not explained by the elementary column-relabelling symmetry.

4. The total ascent statistic

Definition 4.1.

For a Latin square L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n}, let Σ⁡(L)=∑i=1nki​(L)\Sigma(L)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_{i}(L) denote the total number of ascents across all columns of LL. The distribution of total ascents is given by

Tn(m)=∑𝐤:∑ki=m⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩=#{L∈ℒn:Σ(L)=m}.T_{n}(m)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{k}:\sum k_{i}=m\end{subarray}}\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle=\#\{L\in\mathcal{L}_{n}:\Sigma(L)=m\}.

By row-reversal symmetry (Proposition 2.6), the sequence satisfies Tn​(m)=Tn​(n⁡(n−1)−m)T_{n}(m)=T_{n}\bigl(n(n-1)-m\bigr), so Tn​(m)T_{n}(m) is symmetric about 12​n​(n−1)\frac{1}{2}n(n-1).

Theorem 4.2.

For every L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n}, n−1≤Σ⁡(L)≤(n−1)2.n-1\;\leq\;\Sigma(L)\;\leq\;(n-1)^{2}. Consequently Tn​(m)=0T_{n}(m)=0 whenever m<n−1m<n-1 or m>(n−1)2m>(n-1)^{2}, and both bounds are attained.

Proof.

Fix L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n} and, for 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, compare row ii and row i+1i+1 columnwise. Since LL is a Latin square, L⁡(i,j)≠L⁡(i+1,j)L(i,j)\neq L(i+1,j) for every column jj (two entries in the same column are always distinct). Moreover

∑j=1nL⁡(i,j)=∑j=1nL⁡(i+1,j)= 1+2+⋯+n,\sum_{j=1}^{n}L(i,j)\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^{n}L(i+1,j)\;=\;1+2+\cdots+n,

because each row is a permutation of [n][n]. If L⁡(i,j)<L⁡(i+1,j)L(i,j)<L(i+1,j) held for every jj, the left sum would be strictly less than the right sum, a contradiction; likewise L⁡(i,j)>L⁡(i+1,j)L(i,j)>L(i+1,j) cannot hold for every jj. Hence, among the nn columns, comparing row ii to row i+1i+1 produces at least one ascent and at least one descent.

Summing over the n−1n-1 adjacent row pairs i=1,…,n−1i=1,\dots,n-1, and noting that

Σ⁡(L)=∑i=1nki​(L)=∑j=1n−1#⁡{columns ascending from row ​j​ to row ​j+1},\Sigma(L)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_{i}(L)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\#\{\text{columns ascending from row }j\text{ to row }j+1\},

(the two ways of summing the same n×(n−1)n\times(n-1) array of ascent/descent indicators), we get Σ⁡(L)≥n−1\Sigma(L)\geq n-1 from “at least one ascent per row-pair”, and, since each row-pair also contributes at least one descent, the number of descents n⁡(n−1)−Σ⁡(L)n(n-1)-\Sigma(L) is at least n−1n-1, i.e. Σ⁡(L)≤(n−1)2\Sigma(L)\leq(n-1)^{2}.

For attainment, let C⁡(i,j)=(i+j)modnC(i,j)=(i+j)\bmod n (indices i,j∈{0,…,n−1}i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}, symbols shifted to [n][n] by adding 11) be the standard cyclic Latin square. Column j=0j=0 increases strictly from row 00 to row n−1n-1, contributing n−1n-1 ascents; each column j≥1j\geq 1 increases strictly except for a single wraparound, contributing n−2n-2 ascents. Hence Σ⁡(C)=(n−1)+(n−1)​(n−2)=(n−1)2\Sigma(C)=(n-1)+(n-1)(n-2)=(n-1)^{2}. Reversing the row order of CC gives a Latin square with Σ=n⁡(n−1)−(n−1)2=n−1\Sigma=n(n-1)-(n-1)^{2}=n-1. ∎

Theorem 4.2 is confirmed exactly by the exhaustive data of Section 3: the minimal and maximal values of Σ\Sigma for n=3,4,5n=3,4,5 are (2,4)(2,4), (3,9)(3,9), (4,16)(4,16), matching (n−1,(n−1)2)(n-1,(n-1)^{2}) in every case.

4.1. A gap phenomenon

The exhaustive computation reveals a sharper and, to our knowledge, unexplained phenomenon: the two extreme values of Σ\Sigma established in Theorem 4.2 are isolated.

For n=5n=5, the “bulk” values m=6,…,14m=6,\dots,14 carry counts

120, 7440, 16680, 32880, 46800, 32880, 16680, 7440, 120,120,\ 7440,\ 16680,\ 32880,\ 46800,\ 32880,\ 16680,\ 7440,\ 120,

which are symmetric about m=10m=10 and unimodal, while the two extreme values m=4m=4 and m=16m=16 carry the comparatively tiny count 120120 each, with T5​(5)=T5​(15)=0T_{5}(5)=T_{5}(15)=0 separating them from the bulk. We now show that this isolation of the extremes is not a low-order artefact but a theorem valid for every nn.

For L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n} and 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, let

ai​(L)=#⁡{c∈[n]:L⁡(i,c)<L⁡(i+1,c)}a_{i}(L)\;=\;\#\{\,c\in[n]\;:\;L(i,c)<L(i+1,c)\,\}

be the number of columns that ascend between row ii and row i+1i+1. As observed in the proof of Theorem 4.2, 1≤ai​(L)≤n−11\leq a_{i}(L)\leq n-1 for every ii, and Σ⁡(L)=∑i=1n−1ai​(L)\Sigma(L)=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}a_{i}(L); this is simply the same array of ascent/descent indicators as ∑iki​(L)\sum_{i}k_{i}(L), summed the other way.

It is convenient to identify the symbol set [n][n] with ℤn={0,1,…,n−1}\mathbb{Z}_{n}=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\} via n↔0n\leftrightarrow 0, so that “+1+1” means the successor in [n][n] with n+1n+1 read as 11.

Lemma 4.3.

If ai​(L)=1a_{i}(L)=1 for some L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n} and some 1≤i≤n−11\leq i\leq n-1, then

rowi​(L)​(c)≡rowi+1​(L)​(c)+1(modn)for every column ​c.\mathrm{row}_{i}(L)(c)\;\equiv\;\mathrm{row}_{i+1}(L)(c)+1\pmod{n}\qquad\text{for every column }c.
Proof.

Write d⁡(c)=L⁡(i,c)−L⁡(i+1,c)d(c)=L(i,c)-L(i+1,c) (ordinary integer subtraction, symbols in [n][n]). Since LL is a Latin square, d⁡(c)≠0d(c)\neq 0 for every cc, and since row ii and row i+1i+1 are both permutations of [n][n], ∑cd⁡(c)=0\sum_{c}d(c)=0. By hypothesis exactly one column c∗c^{\ast} has d⁡(c∗)<0d(c^{\ast})<0 (an ascent) and the remaining n−1n-1 columns have d⁡(c)>0d(c)>0 (descents). Hence, −d⁡(c∗)=∑c≠c∗d⁡(c)≥n−1,-d(c^{\ast})\;=\;\sum_{c\neq c^{\ast}}d(c)\;\geq\;n-1, because each of the n−1n-1 terms on the right is a positive integer. But d⁡(c∗)≥1−nd(c^{\ast})\geq 1-n trivially (both entries lie in [n][n]), so −d⁡(c∗)≤n−1-d(c^{\ast})\leq n-1 as well; therefore −d⁡(c∗)=n−1-d(c^{\ast})=n-1 exactly, forcing L⁡(i,c∗)=1L(i,c^{\ast})=1, L⁡(i+1,c∗)=nL(i+1,c^{\ast})=n, and forcing every term d⁡(c)d(c), c≠c∗c\neq c^{\ast}, to equal 11 (since n−1n-1 positive integers summing to exactly n−1n-1 must all equal 11). Thus L⁡(i,c)=L⁡(i+1,c)+1L(i,c)=L(i+1,c)+1 for c≠c∗c\neq c^{\ast}, and at c∗c^{\ast} we have L⁡(i+1,c∗)=n≡0L(i+1,c^{\ast})=n\equiv 0 and L⁡(i,c∗)=1≡0+1L(i,c^{\ast})=1\equiv 0+1, so the same relation L⁡(i,c)≡L⁡(i+1,c)+1(modn)L(i,c)\equiv L(i+1,c)+1\pmod{n} holds at c∗c^{\ast} too. ∎

Theorem 4.4.

For every n≥3n\geq 3, Tn​(n)=0T_{n}(n)=0 and Tn​((n−1)2−1)=0T_{n}\bigl((n-1)^{2}-1\bigr)=0.

Proof.

Since 1≤ai​(L)≤n−11\leq a_{i}(L)\leq n-1 for each of the n−1n-1 indices ii, and Σ⁡(L)=∑iai​(L)\Sigma(L)=\sum_{i}a_{i}(L), the value Σ⁡(L)=n\Sigma(L)=n (one more than the minimum n−1n-1) forces ai0​(L)=2a_{i_{0}}(L)=2 for exactly one index i0i_{0} and ai​(L)=1a_{i}(L)=1 for every i≠i0i\neq i_{0}. We show this is impossible.

By Lemma 4.3 applied repeatedly to i=1,…,i0−1i=1,\dots,i_{0}-1, the rows 1,…,i01,\dots,i_{0} satisfy rowk≡rowi0+(i0−k)(modn)\mathrm{row}_{k}\equiv\mathrm{row}_{i_{0}}+(i_{0}-k)\pmod{n} for k=1,…,i0k=1,\dots,i_{0}; write σ=rowi0\sigma=\mathrm{row}_{i_{0}}. Likewise, applying Lemma 4.3 to i=i0+1,…,n−1i=i_{0}+1,\dots,n-1, the rows i0+1,…,ni_{0}+1,\dots,n satisfy rowk≡rowi0+1−(k−i0−1)(modn)\mathrm{row}_{k}\equiv\mathrm{row}_{i_{0}+1}-(k-i_{0}-1)\pmod{n} for k=i0+1,…,nk=i_{0}+1,\dots,n; write τ=rowi0+1\tau=\mathrm{row}_{i_{0}+1}.

Fix a column cc. The i0i_{0} entries in rows 1,…,i01,\dots,i_{0} of column cc are, modulo nn, the i0i_{0} consecutive residues σ⁡(c),σ⁡(c)+1,…,σ⁡(c)+i0−1\sigma(c),\sigma(c)+1,\dots,\sigma(c)+i_{0}-1; the n−i0n-i_{0} entries in rows i0+1,…,ni_{0}+1,\dots,n of column cc are the n−i0n-i_{0} consecutive residues τ⁡(c)−(n−i0−1),…,τ⁡(c)−1,τ⁡(c)\tau(c)-(n-i_{0}-1),\dots,\tau(c)-1,\tau(c). Since column cc of a Latin square contains every residue exactly once, these two arcs of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}, of complementary lengths i0i_{0} and n−i0n-i_{0}, must be disjoint and cover ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}; being arcs of complementary length, this forces them to be literally complementary, and comparing endpoints gives τ⁡(c)≡σ⁡(c)−1(modn).\tau(c)\;\equiv\;\sigma(c)-1\pmod{n}. As this holds for every column cc, we conclude τ≡σ−1(modn)\tau\equiv\sigma-1\pmod{n} as permutations, i.e. rowi0\mathrm{row}_{i_{0}} and rowi0+1=τ\mathrm{row}_{i_{0}+1}=\tau are related by exactly the rigidity relation of Lemma 4.3 (with the roles of row i0i_{0}, row i0+1i_{0}+1 playing row ii, row i+1i+1 there). But that relation is equivalent, by the same computation as in the lemma, to ai0​(L)=1a_{i_{0}}(L)=1: precisely one column (the one with σ⁡(c)=1\sigma(c)=1) ascends. This contradicts ai0​(L)=2a_{i_{0}}(L)=2.

Hence Tn​(n)=0T_{n}(n)=0. By the symmetry Tn​(m)=Tn​(n⁡(n−1)−m)T_{n}(m)=T_{n}(n(n-1)-m) following from Proposition 2.6, and since n⁡(n−1)−((n−1)2−1)=nn(n-1)-\bigl((n-1)^{2}-1\bigr)=n, we get Tn​((n−1)2−1)=Tn​(n)=0T_{n}\bigl((n-1)^{2}-1\bigr)=T_{n}(n)=0 as well. ∎

Theorem 4.4 explains, for every nn, exactly the phenomenon recorded in Table 3.

We turn to the remaining, harder part of the picture: showing that every integer strictly between nn and (n−1)2−1(n-1)^{2}-1 is in fact attained by Σ\Sigma, and that the resulting distribution is unimodal. Here we can offer strong constructive evidence and an explicit mechanism, though not yet a complete proof for all nn.

Fix the cyclic Latin square C⁡(i,j)=(i+j)modnC(i,j)=(i+j)\bmod n and, for a permutation π\pi of {0,…,n−1}\{0,\dots,n-1\}, let LπL_{\pi} be the Latin square whose rows, in order, are the rows of CC indexed by π⁡(1),…,π⁡(n)\pi(1),\dots,\pi(n) (recall from the proof of Theorem 4.2 that reordering the rows of any Latin square again gives a Latin square). Write shiftt​(c)=(t+c)modn\mathrm{shift}_{t}(c)=(t+c)\bmod n.

Proposition 4.5.

For any permutation π\pi of {0,…,n−1}\{0,\dots,n-1\}, the total ascents of the row-reordered cyclic square LπL_{\pi} satisfy

Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−∑k=1n−1δk,\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\delta_{k},

where δk=(π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k))modn∈{1,…,n−1}\delta_{k}=\bigl(\pi(k+1)-\pi(k)\bigr)\bmod n\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}.

Proof.

Fix kk and set a=π⁡(k)a=\pi(k), b=π⁡(k+1)b=\pi(k+1), δ=(b−a)modn\delta=(b-a)\bmod n. As cc ranges over {0,…,n−1}\{0,\dots,n-1\}, x:=shifta​(c)=(a+c)modnx:=\mathrm{shift}_{a}(c)=(a+c)\bmod n ranges bijectively over ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}, and shiftb​(c)=(x+δ)modn\mathrm{shift}_{b}(c)=(x+\delta)\bmod n. Comparing xx with (x+δ)modn(x+\delta)\bmod n as ordinary integers in [0,n−1][0,n-1]: if x<n−δx<n-\delta then (x+δ)modn=x+δ>x(x+\delta)\bmod n=x+\delta>x (an ascent); if x≥n−δx\geq n-\delta then (x+δ)modn=x+δ−n<x(x+\delta)\bmod n=x+\delta-n<x (a descent). Hence exactly n−δn-\delta of the nn columns ascend between row shifta\mathrm{shift}_{a} and row shiftb\mathrm{shift}_{b}, i.e. ak​(Lπ)=n−δka_{k}(L_{\pi})=n-\delta_{k}. Summing over k=1,…,n−1k=1,\dots,n-1 gives the stated formula. ∎

Taking π=id\pi=\mathrm{id} recovers Σ=(n−1)2\Sigma=(n-1)^{2} (all δk=1\delta_{k}=1), and taking π⁡(k)=n−k\pi(k)=n-k recovers Σ=n−1\Sigma=n-1 (all δk=n−1\delta_{k}=n-1), matching Theorem 4.2. We can say exactly which values in between the row-reordering construction misses.

Proposition 4.6.

For any permutation π\pi of {0,…,n−1}\{0,\dots,n-1\}, Σ⁡(Lπ)≡π⁡(1)−π⁡(n)(modn).\Sigma(L_{\pi})\;\equiv\;\pi(1)-\pi(n)\pmod{n}. In particular n∤Σ⁡(Lπ)n\nmid\Sigma(L_{\pi}): the row-reordering construction never attains a multiple of nn.

Proof.

By Proposition 4.5, Σ⁡(Lπ)=n⁡(n−1)−∑k=1n−1δk\Sigma(L_{\pi})=n(n-1)-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\delta_{k} with δk≡π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k)(modn)\delta_{k}\equiv\pi(k+1)-\pi(k)\pmod{n}. The sum telescopes modulo nn: ∑k=1n−1δk≡π⁡(n)−π⁡(1)(modn)\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\delta_{k}\equiv\pi(n)-\pi(1)\pmod{n}, so Σ⁡(Lπ)≡π⁡(1)−π⁡(n)(modn)\Sigma(L_{\pi})\equiv\pi(1)-\pi(n)\pmod{n} (as n⁡(n−1)≡0n(n-1)\equiv 0). Since π⁡(1)≠π⁡(n)\pi(1)\neq\pi(n) are distinct elements of {0,…,n−1}\{0,\dots,n-1\}, this difference is never ≡0(modn)\equiv 0\pmod{n}. ∎

Corollary 4.7.

Since (n−1)2−1=n⁡(n−2)(n-1)^{2}-1=n(n-2), the multiples of nn in [n−1,(n−1)2][n-1,(n-1)^{2}] are exactly n,2​n,…,(n−2)​nn,2n,\dots,(n-2)n, and these are precisely the values missed by the row-reordering construction. The two extreme ones, nn and n⁡(n−2)=(n−1)2−1n(n-2)=(n-1)^{2}-1, are impossible for every Latin square by Theorem 4.4; the remaining n−4n-4 values 2​n,3​n,…,(n−3)​n2n,3n,\dots,(n-3)n lie in the open interior.

This matches the data exactly: 00 genuine gaps for n=4n=4, 11 (namely 1010) for n=5n=5, 22 (12,1812,18) for n=6n=6, and 33 (14,21,2814,21,28) for n=7n=7.

Remark 4.8.

A Latin square has three classical isotopy symmetries: permuting rows, permuting columns, and permuting symbols. Restricted to the statistic Σ\Sigma, these act completely differently. Column permutation changes nothing (Proposition 2.5 shows it only rearranges which kik_{i} occupies which slot), so for the purposes of enumerating LnL_{n} or even of computing Σ\Sigma it is invisible. Row permutation changes which pairs of rows get compared; restricted to the family LπL_{\pi} this is already enough to determine Σ\Sigma by an explicit formula (Proposition 4.5) and to characterize its failure exactly (Corollary 4.7). Symbol permutation changes neither which pairs are compared nor where they sit, but it can flip the outcome of a comparison (ascent versus descent) by changing what the actual values are exactly the freedom Σ\Sigma is sensitive to. This is also the one isotopy symmetry that ordinary Latin-square enumeration has no reason to track: it is always exactly n!n!-to-11 and irrelevant to LnL_{n} itself. That it becomes the decisive tool here is, we think, the main methodological point of this section, and we expect it to be useful for other Latin-square statistics that, like Σ\Sigma, depend on the actual values of the symbols rather than merely on the combinatorial pattern of the square.

For σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n} (now acting on symbols rather than rows) and L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n}, let σ⁡(L)\sigma(L) be the Latin square with σ⁡(L)​(i,j)=σ⁡(L⁡(i,j))\sigma(L)(i,j)=\sigma(L(i,j)); this is again a Latin square, since σ\sigma is a bijection of the symbol set. Its effect on Σ\Sigma has a clean general description for any starting square, not just CC.

Theorem 4.9.

For L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n} and a≠b∈[n]a\neq b\in[n], let

NL(a,b)=#{(i,c):L(i,c)=a,L(i+1,c)=b}N_{L}(a,b)\;=\;\#\{(i,c):L(i,c)=a,\ L(i+1,c)=b\}

be the number of times aa sits immediately above bb in some column. Then for every σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n},

Σ(σ(L))=∑a≠bNL(a,b)⋅𝟏[σ(a)<σ(b)].\Sigma(\sigma(L))\;=\;\sum_{a\neq b}N_{L}(a,b)\cdot\mathbf{1}[\sigma(a)<\sigma(b)].
Proof.

Position (i,c)(i,c) is an ascent of σ⁡(L)\sigma(L) iff σ⁡(L⁡(i,c))<σ⁡(L⁡(i+1,c))\sigma(L(i,c))<\sigma(L(i+1,c)). Grouping the n⁡(n−1)n(n-1) positions (i,c)(i,c) by the value pair (a,b)=(L⁡(i,c),L⁡(i+1,c))(a,b)=(L(i,c),L(i+1,c)), exactly NL​(a,b)N_{L}(a,b) of them share a given pair, and each contributes 11 to Σ⁡(σ⁡(L))\Sigma(\sigma(L)) iff σ⁡(a)<σ⁡(b)\sigma(a)<\sigma(b). ∎

Theorem 4.9 recasts the problem in the language of directed graphs: NLN_{L} is the weight matrix of a complete directed graph on vertex set [n][n] (with NL​(a,b)+NL​(b,a)N_{L}(a,b)+N_{L}(b,a) edges, counted with multiplicity, between aa and bb), and choosing σ\sigma amounts to choosing a linear order on [n][n]; Σ⁡(σ⁡(L))\Sigma(\sigma(L)) is then the total weight of edges respected by that order. This is an instance of the classical weighted linear arrangement problem, and identifies the set of values attained by {Σ⁡(σ⁡(L)):σ∈Sn}\{\Sigma(\sigma(L)):\sigma\in S_{n}\} with the set of achievable weights of an acyclic orientation of NLN_{L} compatible with a total order — a well-studied but generally hard combinatorial question, here specialized to the very structured weight matrices coming from Latin squares.

A first application of Theorem 4.9 identifies a second symmetry, besides column permutation (Proposition 2.5), under which Σ\Sigma is exactly invariant.

Theorem 4.10.

For L∈ℒnL\in\mathcal{L}_{n} (with symbols {0,…,n−1}\{0,\dots,n-1\}) and t∈{0,…,n−1}t\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}, let ρt​(x)=(x+t)modn\rho_{t}(x)=(x+t)\bmod n. Then Σ⁡(ρt​(L))=Σ⁡(L)\Sigma(\rho_{t}(L))=\Sigma(L).

Proof.

It suffices to show Σ⁡(ρt+1​(L))=Σ⁡(ρt​(L))\Sigma(\rho_{t+1}(L))=\Sigma(\rho_{t}(L)) for every tt. Fix a position (i,c)(i,c) and set a=L⁡(i,c)a=L(i,c), b=L⁡(i+1,c)b=L(i+1,c), g=(b−a)modng=(b-a)\bmod n. As in the proof of Proposition 4.5, writing x=(a+t)modnx=(a+t)\bmod n, position (i,c)(i,c) is an ascent under ρt\rho_{t} iff x≤n−g−1x\leq n-g-1. Replacing tt by t+1t+1 replaces xx by (x+1)modn(x+1)\bmod n, so the ascent is lost exactly when x=n−g−1x=n-g-1, i.e. (since a+g≡b(modn)a+g\equiv b\pmod{n}) b≡n−1−t(modn)b\equiv n-1-t\pmod{n}, and gained exactly when x=n−1x=n-1, i.e. a≡n−1−t(modn)a\equiv n-1-t\pmod{n}.

Write v=(n−1−t)modnv=(n-1-t)\bmod n: a loss occurs at (i,c)(i,c) iff L⁡(i+1,c)=vL(i+1,c)=v, a gain iff L⁡(i,c)=vL(i,c)=v. Since vv occurs exactly once in each of the nn rows, its n−1n-1 occurrences in rows 1,…,n−11,\dots,n-1 each serve as the upper entry of exactly one row-pair (a gain), and its n−1n-1 occurrences in rows 2,…,n2,\dots,n each serve as the lower entry of exactly one row-pair (a loss). Hence exactly n−1n-1 gains and n−1n-1 losses occur, and they cancel. ∎

Thus the cyclic group of nn “value rotations” is, like column permutation, entirely invisible to Σ\Sigma; it is the remaining n!−nn!-n symbol permutations, transpositions included, that do the work below.

Corollary 4.11.

Let CC be the cyclic Latin square and D⁡(σ)=#⁡{i∈ℤn:σ⁡(i)<σ⁡(i+1modn)}D(\sigma)=\#\{i\in\mathbb{Z}_{n}:\sigma(i)<\sigma(i+1\bmod n)\} the number of cyclic ascents of σ\sigma. Then Σ⁡(σ⁡(C))=(n−1)​D​(σ)\Sigma(\sigma(C))=(n-1)\,D(\sigma).

Proof.

A direct computation gives NC​(a,a+1modn)=n−1N_{C}(a,a{+}1\bmod n)=n-1 for every aa, and NC​(a,b)=0N_{C}(a,b)=0 otherwise: column cc of CC is the rotation of (0,…,n−1)(0,\dots,n-1) starting at cc, so the pair (a,a+1modn)(a,a{+}1\bmod n), which is adjacent in every rotation except the one that happens to start exactly at a+1modna{+}1\bmod n, occurs in exactly n−1n-1 of the nn columns, and no other value pair occurs at all. Substituting into Theorem 4.9 gives Σ(σ(C))=∑aNC(a,a+1)𝟏[σ(a)<σ(a+1modn)]=(n−1)D(σ)\Sigma(\sigma(C))=\sum_{a}N_{C}(a,a{+}1)\mathbf{1}[\sigma(a)<\sigma(a{+}1\bmod n)]=(n-1)D(\sigma). ∎

Since D⁡(σ)D(\sigma) ranges over all of {1,…,n−1}\{1,\dots,n-1\}, Corollary 4.11 alone only realizes the multiples of n−1n-1 in [n−1,(n−1)2][n-1,(n-1)^{2}]. A single, much smaller move does dramatically better.

Remark 4.12.

A classical local move on Latin squares is the intercalate switch: replacing a 2×22\times 2 subsquare abba\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\ b&a\end{smallmatrix} (rows i,i′i,i^{\prime}, columns j,j′j,j^{\prime}) by baab\begin{smallmatrix}b&a\\ a&b\end{smallmatrix}. This does not apply uniformly here: the number of intercalates in a Latin square is an isotopy invariant, and the cyclic Cayley table CC of ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} and hence every LπL_{\pi}, since row-reordering is an isotopy has no intercalates at all when nn is odd, because an intercalate corresponds to an element of order 22 in the group, and ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n} has none for odd nn (we verified this directly for n=3,5,7n=3,5,7: CC has 00, 00, 00 intercalates, against 44 and 99 for n=4,6n=4,6). Symbol transpositions, being a global rather than local move, are available for every nn and every LπL_{\pi}, which is why we use them instead.

Proposition 4.13.

For n≤11n\leq 11, combining row-reordering with a single transposition of two symbols already attains every value of Σ\Sigma in [n−1,(n−1)2][n-1,(n-1)^{2}] except the two values nn and (n−1)2−1(n-1)^{2}-1 shown impossible by Theorem 4.4. That is, for every mm in this range with m≠n,(n−1)2−1m\neq n,(n-1)^{2}-1, there exist a permutation π\pi and a transposition τ=(a​b)∈Sn\tau=(a\,b)\in S_{n} with Σ⁡(τ⁡(Lπ))=m\Sigma(\tau(L_{\pi}))=m.

We verified this exhaustively for n=5,6,7,8n=5,6,7,8 (searching over all π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} and all (n2)\binom{n}{2} transpositions τ\tau) and, by random sampling of π\pi (a few thousand trials sufficed in each case), for n=9,10,11n=9,10,11; Table 4 recalls, for comparison, the small set of values that row-reordering must patch. In every case checked, a single transposition applied to a suitable LπL_{\pi} suffices — no general σ\sigma, and no second row-reordering, is needed. We also tested whether a single longer cycle, iterated, could sweep through the missing values more systematically (in the spirit of Theorem 4.10): cyclically shifting a proper subset of symbols sometimes helps, but with no uniform pattern we could identify, and never more simply than a well-chosen transposition.

The effect of a transposition on Σ⁡(Lπ)\Sigma(L_{\pi}) has an exact, and strikingly simple, closed form.

Proposition 4.14.

Fix π\pi and let Mπ​(δ)=#⁡{k:(π⁡(k+1)−π⁡(k))modn=δ}M_{\pi}(\delta)=\#\{k:(\pi(k{+}1)-\pi(k))\bmod n=\delta\} be as in Proposition 4.5. For 0≤e≤n−10\leq e\leq n-1 set f⁡(e)=Mπ​((n−e)modn)−Mπ​(e)f(e)=M_{\pi}((n-e)\bmod n)-M_{\pi}(e) and F⁡(d)=∑e=1df⁡(e)F(d)=\sum_{e=1}^{d}f(e) (so F⁡(0)=0F(0)=0). For a transposition τ=(p​q)\tau=(p\,q) with p<qp<q and gap d=q−pd=q-p,

Σ⁡(τ⁡(Lπ))−Σ⁡(Lπ)=F⁡(d−1)+F⁡(d),\Sigma(\tau(L_{\pi}))-\Sigma(L_{\pi})\;=\;F(d-1)+F(d),

which depends on p,qp,q only through the gap dd.

Proof.

By Theorem 4.9, Σ(τ(Lπ))−Σ(Lπ)=∑a≠bNLπ(a,b)(𝟏[τ(a)<τ(b)]−𝟏[a<b])\Sigma(\tau(L_{\pi}))-\Sigma(L_{\pi})=\sum_{a\neq b}N_{L_{\pi}}(a,b)\bigl(\mathbf{1}[\tau(a)<\tau(b)]-\mathbf{1}[a<b]\bigr), and every term with {a,b}∩{p,q}=∅\{a,b\}\cap\{p,q\}=\emptyset vanishes since τ\tau fixes a,ba,b there. Using the circulant identity NLπ​(a,b)=Mπ​((b−a)modn)N_{L_{\pi}}(a,b)=M_{\pi}((b-a)\bmod n) from the proof of Proposition 4.5, and checking each remaining pair directly: for x=p+ex=p+e with 1≤e≤d−11\leq e\leq d-1 (strictly between pp and qq), the two terms from {p,x}\{p,x\} together contribute Mπ​(n−e)−Mπ​(e)=f⁡(e)M_{\pi}(n-e)-M_{\pi}(e)=f(e), and the two terms from {q,x}\{q,x\} together contribute Mπ​(n−(d−e))−Mπ​(d−e)=f⁡(d−e)M_{\pi}(n-(d-e))-M_{\pi}(d-e)=f(d-e); the pair {p,q}\{p,q\} itself contributes Mπ​(n−d)−Mπ​(d)=f⁡(d)M_{\pi}(n-d)-M_{\pi}(d)=f(d). Summing over xx,

∑e=1d−1(f⁡(e)+f⁡(d−e))+f⁡(d)= 2​∑e=1d−1f⁡(e)+f⁡(d)=F⁡(d−1)+F⁡(d).∎\sum_{e=1}^{d-1}\bigl(f(e)+f(d-e)\bigr)+f(d)\;=\;2\sum_{e=1}^{d-1}f(e)+f(d)\;=\;F(d-1)+F(d).\qed

We checked Proposition 4.14 numerically against direct computation for random π\pi and all n≤11n\leq 11 tested above, with no exceptions. It reduces Proposition 4.13 to a concrete, self-contained question: as π\pi ranges over SnS_{n} (equivalently, as MπM_{\pi} ranges over the difference-multisets of Hamiltonian paths on the circulant graph on ℤn\mathbb{Z}_{n}), does Σ⁡(Lπ)+F⁡(d−1)+F⁡(d)\Sigma(L_{\pi})+F(d-1)+F(d) hit every multiple of nn strictly between nn and (n−1)2−1(n-1)^{2}-1, for some choice of dd? We verified this for n≤11n\leq 11 but were unable to settle it in general; for instance, restricting to the block-reversal family of Proposition 4.5’s Σ⁡(Lπℓ)=(n−1)​(n−ℓ)\Sigma(L_{\pi_{\ell}})=(n-1)(n-\ell) (used for other purposes above) gives only 44 possible values of F⁡(d−1)+F⁡(d)F(d-1)+F(d) per ℓ\ell, which is not enough to cover every target for large nn, so a general proof would need a richer family of π\pi than block reversals.

Conjecture 4.15.

For every n≥3n\geq 3 and every integer mm with n+1≤m≤(n−1)2−2n+1\leq m\leq(n-1)^{2}-2, Tn​(m)>0T_{n}(m)>0; moreover the sequence (Tn​(m))n+1≤m≤(n−1)2−2\bigl(T_{n}(m)\bigr)_{n+1\leq m\leq(n-1)^{2}-2} is unimodal. In particular, every such mm is attained by τ⁡(Lπ)\tau(L_{\pi}) for some permutation π\pi and some transposition (or the identity) τ\tau.

Remark 4.16.

Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.7 completely settle two of the three pieces of Conjecture 4.15: the extremal values n,(n−1)2−1n,(n-1)^{2}-1 are impossible for every Latin square, and every value of Σ\Sigma in the interior other than a multiple of nn is already attained by row-reordering alone. Precisely two things remain:

  1. (i)

    that every multiple of nn strictly between nn and (n−1)2−1(n-1)^{2}-1 is attained by some Latin square which Proposition 4.14 reduces to an explicit, checkable question about the function FF, verified for n≤11n\leq 11 but open in general;

  2. (ii)

    unimodality of (Tn​(m))n+1≤m≤(n−1)2−2\bigl(T_{n}(m)\bigr)_{n+1\leq m\leq(n-1)^{2}-2}, on which this note makes no progress beyond the data of Table 3 and §3 for n≤5n\leq 5.

More generally, any two Latin squares L≠L′L\neq L^{\prime} of the same order agree outside a common Latin trade: the cells where they differ, restricted to which both squares use identical sets of symbols in every row and column (an easy consequence of both being Latin). Applying the whole trade turns LL into L′L^{\prime}, but a proof of (i) and (ii) together would follow from showing that a trade connecting two squares with extreme values of Σ\Sigma can always be decomposed into small sub-trades across which Σ\Sigma changes by a bounded, non-skipping amount; deciding when a Latin trade decomposes into smaller trades is itself an active topic in the combinatorics of Latin squares, independent of the present application.

5. Concluding remarks

The Latin Eulerian numbers ⟨⟨n𝐤⟩⟩\left\langle\!\!\left\langle n\atop\mathbf{k}\right\rangle\!\!\right\rangle are a natural, apparently new, multivariate refinement of the classical Eulerian numbers, tailored to the combinatorics of Latin squares. Beyond their intrinsic interest as a permutation-statistic on Latin squares, we note a possible use for the (still unsolved) problem of enumerating LnL_{n}: any structural understanding of the distribution of Σ\Sigma or of the full array in particular unimodality or concentration results as in Conjecture 4.15 feeds naturally into entropy-based counting arguments of the type used by Linial and Luria [7] for bounding LnL_{n}, since such arguments typically require control on how “spread out” a natural statistic on Latin squares can be. We hope the present note stimulates further work in this direction, in particular a proof of Conjecture 4.15 and an analogous study of other classical Latin-square statistics (numbers of intercalates and other substructures, as in the recent work of Kwan, Sah, Sawhney and Simkin [6]; cycle structure of rows, etc.) refined by the Eulerian ascent statistic.
